academicTheory.hypothesis: Lab Learner reliably computes totals from equal groups on rehearsed material; it remains untested whether that reasoning inverts — whether he can recover an unknown factor from a given total on unseen number families, and whether he can reject a total that admits no equal split rather than forcing one. The Quest tests the inversion and the rejection.
falsifyCriteria: Repeated fresh independent errors contradict transfer.

nodes.title: The Lantern Barge Won't Wait

academicTarget.skill: math.multiplication.transfer — specifically missing-factor reasoning from a known total (total ÷ known factor = unknown factor), interpreting word-problem situations where the unknown is group size or group count rather than the product, and recognizing totals that admit no equal split into the requested number of groups.

nodes.mechanic: Loading puzzle with destructive consequence: the child drags a fixed pile of lanterns into a set number of barge racks, and any rack that doesn't match the others tips into the river when the barge launches.
nodes.theme: A night river festival. Lantern barges launch on a schedule down a dark canal. Balanced barges glow all the way to the sea gate; unbalanced ones capsize and go dark in the water.

openingScreen.title: The Lantern Barge Won't Wait
openingScreen.purpose: Open on the dock with one barge already loaded correctly and glowing, and one already capsized and dark beside it — so before a single word of instruction, the child sees that equal groups float and unequal groups sink. The first screen states the stake visually, not verbally.

generationPrompt.text: Build a five-round night-river loading game for a nine-year-old who has already proven he can compute totals from equal groups and can find a missing factor when it is handed to him as a clean number sentence. Do not hand him number sentences. Hand him a pile and a constraint. Round structure: a dockmaster calls out a job in plain speech — "Forty-two lanterns, seven racks, every rack the same" — and the child sees the loose pile of lanterns and the empty racks. The child drags lanterns onto racks; lanterns snap in and the rack shows its running count. The child taps LAUNCH when the barge is loaded. On launch, the barge slides down the canal: if every rack holds the same number and the pile is empty, the lanterns catch, the canal lights up, and the barge passes the sea gate. If racks are uneven or lanterns are left on the dock, the barge lists, racks slide, and lanterns hiss out in the water — those lanterns are gone from the night's total and the dock's tally drops. Escalate the unknown across rounds: round one gives the rack count and the child must find how many per rack; round two gives the per-rack limit and the child must decide how many racks to set out; round three uses an unseen number family (sevens, eights, twelves) so no rehearsed pair rescues him; round four is the trap — the dockmaster calls a job that cannot be done, like fifty lanterns into six equal racks, and the only winning move is to hit the REFUSE JOB rope and tell the dockmaster how many are left over. Launching that barge anyway costs the most lanterns of any round. Round five is a double order under a lantern shortage: two barges, one shared pile, and only enough lanterns if both splits are exact on the first attempt. Give the dockmaster a voice with real opinions — she is not a narrator, she is a woman with a schedule and a river. Log every proposed split, including wrong ones, before the launch resolves. Keep the whole run under six minutes. Regenerate all numbers on replay, because this child asked to play the last thing again. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner reliably computes totals from equal groups on rehearsed material; it remains untested whether that reasoning inverts — whether he can recover an unknown factor from a given total on unseen number families, and whether he can reject a total that admits no equal split rather than forcing one. The Quest tests the inversion and the rejection. This node must test unseen transfer: change the context while preserving the construct. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: All three baseline items were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.0, above the preregistered 0.7–1.0 band), and the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization error never appeared. But every observation carries exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice, so this is rehearsed performance, not transfer. The hypothesis is about fresh material and no fresh material was administered; practice can justify a transfer test but cannot confirm it. Baseline Quest eligibility is met with 3 independent correct readings, so the correct move is to spend that eligibility on genuinely unseen material: a Quest where equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem interpretation must be run in reverse and under a constraint the child has never met — a fixed total that must be split into equal groups, where a wrong split visibly breaks. Engagement evidence is thin (one 5/5 rating, one replay request, 96s duration) — enough to say the child re-entered willingly, not enough to shape presentation, so I am choosing the form on craft grounds and holding it accountable to the mathematics. design.stakes: Lanterns are a finite, visible resource and the child is trying to light the whole canal to the sea gate. Every capsized barge permanently destroys those lanterns — the dock tally drops and does not come back, and the canal ends the night with a dark stretch the child can see. A run with three sinkings ends with the sea gate unlit and the dockmaster saying plainly that the festival was short. Winning is not a checkmark; it is a fully lit river and a specific number the child earned. Losing is not a retry prompt; it is a darker river than the one he could have had, and he has to look at it before he replays.
design.failureMode: A run fails when the child launches unbalanced or incomplete barges enough times that the lantern supply cannot reach the sea gate — the festival ends dark. The specific and most costly failure is round four: forcing an impossible split rather than refusing the job. The child can also fail round five by getting the first split right and the second wrong, because the shared pile leaves no slack. Failure is real, visible, and unrecoverable within a run; the child recovers only by starting the night over with new numbers.
design.escalation: Round one: rack count known, group size unknown, familiar small numbers, generous pile. Round two: the unknown flips to the number of racks, and the child must set out the racks himself before loading. Round three: unseen number families, so rehearsed pairs give no help. Round four: an impossible job arrives with no warning and refusing it is the only correct action — the dockmaster keeps calling for the launch, so the child must hold his ground against pressure. Round five: two barges from one pile with zero surplus, so both splits must be exact on the first attempt and there is no room to test-and-fix.
design.mechanicSpec: The child's finger drags lanterns from a glowing pile at the bottom of the screen onto numbered racks on the barge deck; each lantern snaps into a slot with a soft click and the rack's count ticks up above it. Racks holding different amounts visibly sit at different heights, so imbalance is readable as a tilted deck before launch. A LAUNCH rope hangs at the right; pulling it commits. On a good launch the barge glides, every lantern flares, and the canal ahead lights in a running wave to the sea gate. On a bad launch the deck tips toward the heavy side, racks slide off, lanterns hit the water with a hiss and go out one by one, and the dock tally at the top counts down in front of the child. A REFUSE JOB rope hangs at the left and is live in every round, but only round four rewards it — pulling it opens a small slate where the child types the leftover count, and a wrong leftover still costs lanterns.
design.mathematicalHook: The moment a child discovers that some numbers simply refuse to be shared out evenly — that fifty lanterns and six racks is not a hard problem but an impossible one, and the mature move is to say no and name the two left over. Multiplication stops being a machine that always produces an answer and becomes a question about which totals a number can even build. That flip, from "compute it" to "can this be built at all," is where third-grade multiplication quietly becomes division, factors, and remainders all at once.

nodes.title: Nobody Splits the Last Crate

academicTarget.skill: Synthesis of multiplicative inversion: from a known total, recover an unknown group count or an unknown group size when the word problem does not say which is missing, and identify totals that cannot be split equally into a demanded number of equal groups — justifying the impossibility rather than rounding, dropping, or forcing a remainder.

nodes.mechanic: A loading-dock crate press where the child drags crates into a fixed number of shipping bays or sets the bay count itself, and must slam a red REFUSE lever on any order whose total cannot fill every bay evenly.
nodes.theme: Night shift at a river cargo dock. Orders come down a conveyor from a impatient dispatcher. Every barge leaves whether Lab Learner is ready or not.

openingScreen.title: Nobody Splits the Last Crate
openingScreen.purpose: Open on a conveyor already moving with one order on it and the REFUSE lever glowing, so the very first thing the child learns is that some orders are supposed to be thrown back — before any correct answer trains him to always find a split.

generationPrompt.text: Build a night-shift cargo dock for a 9-year-old who has already proven he can find a missing factor on unseen numbers. Six orders ride a conveyor toward the barge. Each order is a short dispatcher line, never labeled with what is unknown: sometimes the total and the number of bays are given and the child must set how many crates go in each bay; sometimes the total and crates-per-bay are given and he must set the number of bays; and at least two orders are impossible — the total cannot be divided evenly into the demanded bays (for example 26 crates into 4 bays, 45 crates into 6 bays). For those, the only correct action is slamming the REFUSE lever, and the dock ledger asks him to name the two totals nearby that WOULD have worked. Use unseen number families beyond 5×6 and 6×4 — go into 7s, 8s, 9s, and totals up to 90. When he sets a wrong bay count, the crates visibly load and one bay ends up short or overflowing, the barge horn blows, and the order sails with a hole in the manifest. Escalate: order five gives two constraints at once (a total, a minimum crates-per-bay, and a bay count he must choose that satisfies both); order six is the impossible one dressed to look easy. End with the manifest ledger read back to him — every order he shipped, every order he correctly refused, and every hole he left — then let him decide whether he takes tomorrow's shift. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner reliably computes totals from equal groups on rehearsed material; it remains untested whether that reasoning inverts — whether he can recover an unknown factor from a given total on unseen number families, and whether he can reject a total that admits no equal split rather than forcing one. The Quest tests the inversion and the rejection. This node must test unseen synthesis: combine the construct in a context not practised before. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation, unseen.math.multiplication.equal_groups, unseen.math.multiplication.missing_factor, unseen.math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: Quest predicted ≥0.70 fresh unassisted accuracy on inverted multiplicative reasoning; Lab Learner returned 3/3 unseen, unassisted, unconfounded correct readings (accuracy 1.00), and the predicted 'factor-pair overgeneralization' error never appeared. That supports the transfer hypothesis at the level Quest can support it — inversion on unseen number families held. But the Quest responses that were logged ('6 groups of 4 = 24', '7', '5 × 6 = 30') are single-step recoveries, and nothing in the record shows him rejecting a total that admits no equal split, nor coordinating two unknowns under conflicting constraints. Boss eligibility is met with fresh correct unassisted Quest evidence, so the honest next move is unseen synthesis: force him to choose which quantity is unknown, defend a claim that a division is impossible, and pay a real cost when he forces a split that does not exist. design.stakes: The manifest is what is at risk. Each order shipped with an uneven load punches a permanent hole in the night's manifest, and holes are shown in the end-of-shift ledger with the exact order that caused them. Three holes and the dispatcher pulls him off the dock mid-shift — the run ends early, the remaining orders sail without him, and he sees which ones he never got to touch. Refusing an order that was actually shippable also costs: that barge leaves empty and counts as a hole too, so 'refuse everything' is not a hiding place.
design.failureMode: Two ways to lose. Forcing an impossible split — loading 26 crates into 4 bays and shipping it — leaves a visible short bay and a manifest hole. Refusing a shippable order leaves an empty barge and a manifest hole. Three holes ends the shift early with orders still on the conveyor he will never see. This can be failed, and it should be: the whole point is that a child who has been right nine times in a row learns nothing from an instrument that cannot tell him no.
design.escalation: Orders one and two state the total and the bay count — he supplies group size only, conveyor slow. Order three flips the unknown to bay count without announcing it. Order four is the first impossible order, arriving at normal speed with no warning. Order five stacks two constraints so a single bay count must satisfy both a total and a minimum load. Order six is impossible but wears friendly round numbers, and by then the conveyor is fast enough that hesitating costs him the order.
design.mechanicSpec: The child's finger drags a stack of crates from the conveyor onto a numbered bay strip at the bottom of the screen, and pinches or taps a dial to set how many bays open. As he turns the dial the bays physically split apart on screen and the crate stack redistributes live, so an uneven setting shows one bay visibly taller or one bay half-empty before he commits. Committing is a tap on the barge horn. Refusing is a hard drag down on the red REFUSE lever at screen right, which flips the order off the conveyor and back up the ramp. Failure looks like this: the barge pulls away, the camera stays on the short bay with its gap of missing crates, a red hole stamps onto the manifest card in the corner, and the hole count ticks up. At three, the dispatcher's hand comes into frame, the conveyor belt stops, and the remaining order cards slide past greyed out.
design.mathematicalHook: Some numbers simply refuse to be shared out evenly, and you can prove it before you move a single crate — 26 will never fill 4 bays, no matter how you shuffle it, but 24 and 28 will. The whoa is discovering that 'this cannot be done' is a real mathematical answer, and that he can spot it faster than the machine can load it.

preserve: Unassisted answering with zero scaffolds offered by default — the child produced all three baseline answers alone and should keep that room
Short dense sessions: the whole baseline ran in 96 seconds, so the Quest should be minutes, not a worksheet
Concrete situational framing (teams, festivals, real objects) rather than bare number sentences
Replayability — the child chose replay_same, so the Quest must be re-runnable with different numbers
change: Move from previously_practiced items to entirely unseen number families and an unseen problem orientation
Stop asking 'how many total' and start asking 'how many in each group' and 'how many groups' from a fixed total — missing-factor reasoning as the engine, not a side item
Introduce a real cost for a wrong split instead of a scored-and-forgotten answer
Introduce totals that do NOT split evenly, so the child must reject an arrangement rather than force one
Add escalating time-free but resource-limited pressure so later rounds cannot be brute-forced by guessing
testNext: Does equal-groups reasoning survive when the total is given and the factor is unknown (division-as-missing-factor)?
Does the child recognize a total that cannot be split into the requested equal groups, and say so, instead of forcing an uneven arrangement?
Does the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization appear — e.g. asserting 6 rows of 4 works for 28 because 6 and 4 are 'a pair they know'?
Can the child interpret a word-problem situation where the unknown is the group size rather than the product?
Does accuracy hold on unseen number families (7s, 8s, 12s) or was baseline success tied to rehearsed 4s, 5s, 6s?
nextEvidenceRequired: At least 4 unassisted, unseen-item observations linked to math.multiplication.transfer with exposure=unseen and provenance=quest
At least 1 observation where the correct response is a refusal — the child identifies that the total cannot be split evenly and states the leftover
At least 1 observation where the unknown is group size and at least 1 where the unknown is number of groups, scored separately
Error transcripts on any failed split, capturing the specific wrong factor the child proposed, to test the factor-pair overgeneralization prediction
Session-level record of how many crates were lost, to separate 'right on the first try' from 'right after burning attempts'
